Robinson Crusoe was written by Daniel Defoe and first published in 1719. It is often called the first English novel, and it began a whole kind of story: the tale of a person surviving alone against nature by their own wit and effort. This retelling shortens the tale for young readers and presents Crusoe and Friday with equal dignity as friends.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Would Go to Sea

pages.text: I was born in England, and from my earliest years I longed for one thing only: to go to sea. My good father begged me to stay home and live a quiet, sensible life. But I would not listen. Against his wishes, I ran away to sail the oceans, and so began a life of adventure that I would many times wish I had never chosen.

image.note: A young man leaving home for a harbour full of ships, his worried father at the door behind him; the wide sea ahead

pages.text: For years I sailed and traded across the world, meeting both fortune and disaster. Then, on one fateful voyage, a great storm rose up and drove our ship far off course, until at last it struck a hidden reef and began to break apart. The sea poured in, and every soul aboard scrambled for the boats in terror.

image.note: A wooden sailing ship caught in a violent storm, huge waves crashing over the deck; sailors struggling; dramatic

pages.text: The little boat we launched was swamped in an instant by a monstrous wave, and all my companions were lost. I alone was flung, half drowned, onto the shore of an unknown land, and there I lay gasping on the sand as the storm raged on. When at last I lifted my head, I understood the terrible truth. I was utterly, completely alone.

image.note: A single exhausted man washed up on an empty beach, waves behind him, no one else in sight; desolate, alive

pages.text: The next day, the wrecked ship still lay caught upon the reef, not far out. Summoning my courage, I swam and waded to it again and again, and salvaged all I could carry: tools, nails, food, gunpowder, rope, and two cats and a dog that had survived. These few things, saved from the wreck, would become the whole foundation of my new life.

image.note: The man building a raft from planks and barrels, ferrying tools and supplies from the broken ship to shore; resourceful

pages.text: I was master of an island, and prisoner of it too. At first I despaired. I had no company, no hope of rescue, and no idea how long I might be trapped. But despair does not fill a stomach or build a shelter. So I dried my tears, and resolved that if I must live here, I would live as well and as bravely as I possibly could.

image.note: The man sitting alone on a rock at dusk, head bowed, then rising with new resolve; a turn from despair to determination

pages.text: To keep from losing my mind, I did a wise thing. I made a large post and cut a notch in it for every day, and a longer notch for each Sunday, so that I would never lose track of time. I also began to write down all that happened to me. Order and routine, I found, were what kept a lonely man from despair.

image.note: The man carving daily notches into a tall wooden post, a homemade calendar; keeping hold of time and hope

pages.text: Little by little, I built myself a home. I found a cave in a hillside and walled it, and made a strong fence around it against wild beasts. I learned to hunt the wild goats and, cleverer still, to catch and tame them, so that I had a herd of my own for milk and meat. A shipwrecked man, I discovered, can become a farmer.

image.note: The man tending a small herd of tamed goats beside a fenced cave-home built into a hillside; industrious, settled

pages.text: My greatest triumph came by accident. I had shaken out an old sack, and from the few grains left in it, barley and rice sprang up. With enormous patience, over several seasons, I grew these into proper crops, learned to grind the grain, and at last, after much trial and failure, baked my own bread. No feast has ever tasted so sweet.

image.note: The man proudly holding a rough loaf of bread beside a small field of barley; a hard-won triumph; joyful

pages.text: So the years went by, and I grew skilled at my strange, solitary life. I made pots from clay, wove baskets, sewed clothes from goatskins, and even fashioned a wide umbrella against the sun and rain. I had food, shelter and safety. Yet in all that time, one ache never left me: the longing for the sound of another human voice.

image.note: The man in patched goatskin clothes holding a homemade parasol, surveying his tidy island home; capable but lonely

pages.text: I read from a book I had saved from the wreck, and I thought long and hard about my life, my choices, and the father whose wise words I had ignored so long ago. Hardship had made me humble. The proud, restless boy who ran away to sea had become a patient, grateful man who had learned the value of the simplest things.

image.note: The man sitting quietly by lamplight with a worn book, thoughtful and changed; reflection, growth

pages.text: Then, one day, everything changed. Walking along the shore, I stopped as if struck by lightning. There, pressed clearly into the wet sand, was the print of a naked human foot. It was not mine. My heart pounded. After so many years believing myself utterly alone, I now knew, with a shock of both hope and fear, that I was not.

image.note: The man frozen in shock, staring down at a single clear bare footprint in the sand; the loneliest moment broken

pages.text: For a long time I lived in dread, hiding and watching, unsure whether the strangers who sometimes came to my island were friend or foe. I saw that visitors from other islands sometimes landed on my shores, and that they were not always peaceful with one another. I kept myself hidden, and I waited, and I watched.

image.note: The man peering cautiously from behind rocks and bushes at distant figures on a far beach; wary, hidden

pages.text: At last the day came when I saw a man running for his life from others who meant him harm. I chose to act. I rushed out, helped him, and saved him. He fell at my feet in gratitude, and from that day he was my loyal companion. Because I saved him on a Friday, that is the name I gave him, and he called me master.

image.note: The man helping a frightened fleeing islander to safety; the rescued man kneeling in thanks; a friendship begun

pages.text: Friday was clever, brave and kind, and quick to learn. I taught him my language, and he taught me much about the island and the sea. After so many silent years, I finally had a friend to talk to, to work beside, and to share my strange life with. Those were, in truth, among the happiest years I spent upon that lonely shore.

image.note: The two men working and talking together, mending a boat, at ease; companionship, warmth; equals in labour

pages.text: Years later, an English ship anchored off my island. Its crew had mutinied against their captain and set him ashore as a prisoner. Here at last was my chance. Friday and I helped the honest captain overcome the mutineers and win back his ship. In gratitude, the captain gladly offered to carry us home across the sea.

image.note: A ship at anchor; the man and Friday helping a bound captain against rough mutineers on the beach; rescue and alliance

pages.text: I could hardly believe it. After more than twenty-eight years upon that island, I was to leave it at last. I gathered a few keepsakes, my goatskin cap, my old parasol, to remember my long exile by, and with Friday beside me, I boarded the ship. As the island sank behind us into the sea, I felt both a great joy and, to my surprise, a strange sorrow.

image.note: The man and Friday standing at the ship's rail, watching the island shrink on the horizon; joy mixed with wistfulness

pages.text: And so, after twenty-eight years, two months and nineteen days, I came home to England. My parents were long dead, but I was welcomed and, through old ventures, found myself a wealthy man. I had left as a foolish, restless boy, and returned a patient, grateful one, having learned on that island the hardest and finest lessons of my life.

image.note: The weathered older man arriving home in England, greeted warmly; changed, humbled, home at last

pages.text: If my long story teaches anything, it is this. I learned that a person can survive far more than they think, if they keep their head, use their hands, and do not give up hope. And I learned, too late to tell him, that my father had been right all along: that there is deep worth in a steady, thankful life. I never again took such a life for granted.

image.note: The older man sitting content by a warm hearth, telling his tale, Friday nearby; peace, wisdom, closing
